title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, we won’t.
In this analysis, I look at total commuters (travel time table) across counties in Massachusetts (MA), and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. Commuting data (and derivatives of it like ridership information) can dictate where funding goes for transportation infrastructure. This impacts not only a rider’s commute to work, but how they get anywhere in their community.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?

my_variable <- "B08303_001"

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

We can sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                             estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                               <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Dukes County, Massachusetts          8569   846    9.87
 2 Nantucket County, Massachusetts      7068   400    5.66
 3 Franklin County, Massachusetts      29787   730    2.45
 4 Berkshire County, Massachusetts     53440  1303    2.44
 5 Hampshire County, Massachusetts     64314  1441    2.24
 6 Barnstable County, Massachusetts    94875  1658    1.75
 7 Hampden County, Massachusetts      191547  2409    1.26
 8 Suffolk County, Massachusetts      354342  3887    1.10
 9 Norfolk County, Massachusetts      302812  3297    1.09
10 Plymouth County, Massachusetts     229969  2460    1.07


Dukes County is the least reliable county. It has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate (calculated as moe_pct) of 9.87%.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 7 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence     9
2 Low confidence      1
3 Moderate            4


Originally when I had “high confidence” as moe_pct < 5, almost all the counties (12 of 14) fell into that category. Because of this, I changed the variable split to be:
moe_pct < 5 ~ “High confidence”
moe_pct < 10 ~ “Moderate”
This gave a more distributed split of 9 high confidence, 4 moderate, and 1 low confidence.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                             myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                             <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 25001 Barnstable County, Massachusetts  94875   1658 230073    NA
2 25003 Berkshire County, Massachusetts   53440   1303 128047    NA
3 25005 Bristol County, Massachusetts    257154   2658 578436    NA
4 25007 Dukes County, Massachusetts        8569    846  20751    NA
5 25009 Essex County, Massachusetts      353800   3156 807258    NA
6 25011 Franklin County, Massachusetts    29787    730  70922    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now we can compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         12        579779.
2 Moderate                 2         17525 


The average population of high-confidence counties (579779 people) is higher than the average population of moderate counties (17525 people). A general pattern seems to be that the higher the population of a county, the more lower its margin of error.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The data we are looking at comes from the ACS, which is a sample. The smaller the place, the smaller the sample we’ll be able to get. Both Nantucket and Duke County consists of small islands off the southeastern coast of Massachusetts. Nantucket has an estimated population of 14299 and Duke County has an estimated 20751. Compared to Middlesex County with an estimated population of 1622896, it is not surprising that the communities we know the least about are Nantucket and Dukes County. They have the largest margin of error percentages (moe_pct), 5.66% and 9.87% respectively. This is at least 2.19% more than the next largest moe_pct and almost 5% more than Middlsex County, which has the smallest moe_pct. This is in part because of how small Nantucket and Duke County are.
Treating every county’s number as equally certain ignores differences in population, size, community context, and more. If a MA state agency were to allocate funding using the total estimate for travel time to work in the ACS, it would affect each county differently. In this analysis, Nantucket and Duke County could be negatively affected because of how different they are from the rest of Massachusetts. In addition, Nantucket and Dukes County are popular summer vacation spots. The significant summer tourism can impact commute times, both in how long it takes someone to get to work and also what work they are doing. In the off-season, residents may have to travel off-island for work. This requires either a plane or ferry ride, as there are no bridges that connect to either county’s islands. Nantucket and Dukes County residents have to deal with this unconventional commute year-round. The census does not take this into consideration.
We cannot do right by our communities if we take numbers only at face value.

title: Assignment 3 - Verify the Claim
text:
Journalists, agencies, and advocacy organizations publish claims about neighborhood change all the time. Most of those claims rest on American Community Survey (ACS) estimates. Very few of them report margins of error, test whether a change is statistically detectable, or acknowledge what the data cannot support.
In this assignment, I verify claims about poverty rates and median household income in Philadelphia neighborhoods.

title: Assignment 3 - Verify the Claim
section: The Article and What It Claims
text:
The Article and What It Claims
Lubrano, Alfred. “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty.” WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer, December 6, 2018. https://whyy.org/articles/new-census-figures-on-philly-neighborhoods-show-inequality-high-numbers-of-whites-living-in-poverty/
This article compares the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimates and makes several specific claims about poverty rates and median household income in Philadelphia neighborhoods.

the city’s formidable 26 percent poverty rate
“Fairhill in North Philadelphia registered a stunning 61 percent poverty rate.”
The “neighborhood of Eastwick in Southwest Philadelphia, near Philadelphia International Airport, showed the greatest poverty-rate increase of any community, rocketing from 12 percent during 2006-10 to 26 percent in the newest survey.”
White poverty throughout much of the city skyrocketed, led by the Northeast neighborhood of Holmesburg, which went from a 2 percent poverty rate to 19 percent.
The median household income of Tioga-Nicetown plummeted from $28,026 to $17,493, the largest drop in the city.

title: Assignment 3 - Verify the Claim
text:
Part 2 - Testing the Data
Second, we’ll test the data to see if it’s statistically significant or not.
Calculate the poverty rate for each tract and its margin of error. The poverty rate is the percentage of a population whose household income falls below the poverty line, which is set by the government and change by year. The census provides us with the information to be able to calculate this.


Code
philly_tracts_2010 <- philly_tracts_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = 100 * pop_below_poverty_lineE / total_pop_pov_universeE
  )

# drop NA rows
philly_tracts_2010 <- na.omit(philly_tracts_2010)

# do the same for the other dataframe
philly_tracts_2017 <- philly_tracts_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = 100 * pop_below_poverty_lineE / total_pop_pov_universeE
  )

# drop NA rows
philly_tracts_2017 <- na.omit(philly_tracts_2017)

# taking a peek at the data on a map
ggplot(philly_tracts_2010) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = poverty_rate), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::percent) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Poverty Rate In Philadelphia Tracts, ACS 2006-2010 5-Year Estimates",
       fill = NULL)









Calculate the margin of error. The margin of error gibes us a plus-or-minus range. This tells us how much the census survey results may differ from the views of the population. Remember that the ACS is a sample!


Code
philly_tracts_2010 <- philly_tracts_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    moe_prop = moe_prop(pop_below_poverty_lineE, total_pop_pov_universeE, pop_below_poverty_lineM, total_pop_pov_universeM)
  )

philly_tracts_2017 <- philly_tracts_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    moe_prop = moe_prop(pop_below_poverty_lineE, total_pop_pov_universeE, pop_below_poverty_lineM, total_pop_pov_universeM)
)


Compute the coefficient of variation and flag reliability. The coefficient of variation measures the reliability of the data. High reliability (green circle) suggests high precision and consistency in the data (we want this!). Medium reliability (yellow circle) is typically sufficient for general use. Low reliability (red circle) reflects very low trustworthiness. As you’ll see below, the majority of the tracts’ poverty rate have a high reliability.


Code
# drop geometries 
philly_tracts_2010 <- philly_tracts_2010 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() 

philly_tracts_2017 <- philly_tracts_2017 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() 

# calculate cv and make reliability table
reliability_table_2017 <- philly_tracts_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    cv = case_when(TRUE ~ 100 * (moe_prop / 1.645) / poverty_rate),
    dot = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "🟢",
      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE     ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      is.na(cv) ~ NA_character_,
      cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    GEOID,
    dot,
    NAME,
    moe_prop,
    poverty_rate,
    cv,
    flag
  )


reliability_table_2017 %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(moe_prop, poverty_rate),
    decimals = 1
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = cv,
    decimals = 1
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    GEOID = "GEOID",
    dot = "",
    NAME = "Name",
    moe_prop = "Margin of error",
    poverty_rate = "Poverty rate (%)",
    cv = "CV (%)",
    flag = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(
    align = "center",
    columns = c(dot, cv, flag)
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Population Below 100% of the Poverty Level",
    subtitle = "Philadelphia Tracts, ACS 2013–2017 5-year estimates"
  ) %>%

Here, I join the tables together since I start to compute change between the two periods of time.
Compute the change between the two periods and the margin of error of that change. In order to refute or back up the claims made in the article, we need to look at the change between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 in a statistical manner.


Code
# join tables
philly_tract_combined <- left_join(philly_tracts_2017, philly_tracts_2010, by = "GEOID")

#calculating diff in pov rate
philly_tract_combined <- philly_tract_combined %>%
  mutate(diff_poverty_rate = poverty_rate.y-poverty_rate.x)

# calculating standard error
philly_tract_combined <- philly_tract_combined %>%
  mutate(SE2010 = (moe_prop.y*100)/1.645) %>%
  mutate(SE2017 = (moe_prop.x*100)/1.645)

# calculating standard error difference
philly_tract_combined <- philly_tract_combined %>%
  mutate(SE_diff = sqrt((SE2010^2) + (SE2017^2)))

# calculating z-scores
philly_tract_combined <- philly_tract_combined %>%
  mutate(z_score = ((poverty_rate.y-poverty_rate.x)/SE_diff))

philly_tract_combined <- philly_tract_combined %>%
  mutate(
    change   = poverty_rate.y-poverty_rate.x,
    se_1     = (moe_prop.y*100) / 1.645,
    se_2     = (moe_prop.x*100) / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

# visualize with error bars
philly_tract_combined %>%
  filter(significant) %>%
  mutate( NAME.x = str_remove(NAME.x, " Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME.x, diff_poverty_rate), y = diff_poverty_rate)) +
    geom_col(aes(fill = diff_poverty_rate > 0)) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = change - SE_diff,
                      ymax = change + SE_diff), width = 0.2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 4)) +
    labs(title = "Statistically Significant Change in Poverty Rate",
         subtitle = "2013–2017 vs 2006–2010, ACS 5-year estimates for Philadelphia tracts",

text:
Part 4 - Rewriting One of the Article’s Central Paragraph
Fairhill is the poorest neighborhood in Philly. It has an estimated poverty rate of 63.36% with a margin of error of 11.76%. The median household income is estimated to be $13,353 with a margin of error of $3,905. These seem like very alarming figures. However, this did not happen overnight and it doesn’t necessarily reflect the trajectory of the entire city. Historically, Fairhill was a very industrial part of Philly, a manufacturing hub anchored by Germantown Avenue. To lower cost, manufacturing jobs eventually moved away from the city or even overseas. According to Crossroads Philly, it was this economic collapse that has laid the conditions of what we call Fairhill today. While the statistic that Fairhill (or at least an estimation of the census tracts that make it up) has an alarmingly high poverty rate, we must look at it with context.

The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?q=SELECT%20*%20FROM%20septa_routes&format=geojson
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:

Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.485  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)

text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.

m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)

Code
check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}  
# helper function for calculating moran's I
# takes in all_sales and list of predictors, uses k=8 for queen weight
# example on how to call it: moran_i_cv(all_sales, predictors2)
library(sf)
library(spdep)

moran_i_cv <- function(all_sales, predictors, k = 8) {
  train <- all_sales %>%
    filter(split == "train")
  
  formula <- reformulate(
    termlabels = predictors,
    response = "sale_price"
  )
  
  cv_predictions <- cv_pred(formula, train)
  cv_residuals <- train$sale_price - cv_predictions
  
  # Extract coordinates safely whether 'train' is an sf object or standard data frame
  if (inherits(train, "sf")) {
    coords <- st_coordinates(train)
  } else if (all(c("lon", "lat") %in% colnames(train))) {
    coords <- as.matrix(train[, c("lon", "lat")])
  } else {
    stop("`all_sales` must be an 'sf' object or contain 'lon' and 'lat' columns.")
  }
  
  neighbors <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = k))
  weights <- nb2listw(
    neighbors,
    style = "W",
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  
  result <- moran.test(
    cv_residuals,
    weights,
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  
  # Return the Moran's I statistic numeric value
  return(unname(result$estimate["Moran I statistic"]))
}

Load training data and building permits
Building permits come from the City of Chicago’s open-data (SODA) endpoint for dataset ydr8-5enu. No app token is needed, but the API serves 1,000 rows per request, so pages are requested with $limit/$offset in a loop until a short page comes back. The 2023–2025 date range and the two permit types are pushed into the $where clause so only the ~22k relevant rows are downloaded instead of the full 800k+ dataset.


Code
permits_url <- "https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/ydr8-5enu.json"
permits_page_size <- 1000   # rows per request

permits_where <- paste(
  "issue_date >= '2023-01-01T00:00:00' AND issue_date < '2026-01-01T00:00:00'",
  "AND permit_type IN ('PERMIT - NEW CONSTRUCTION', 'PERMIT - RENOVATION/ALTERATION')",
  "AND latitude IS NOT NULL AND longitude IS NOT NULL"
)

fetch_permits_page <- function(offset) {
  resp <- request(permits_url) |>
    req_url_query(
      `$select` = "id,permit_type,issue_date,latitude,longitude",
      `$where` = permits_where,
      `$order` = "id",   # a stable sort keeps page boundaries consistent between requests
      `$limit` = permits_page_size,
      `$offset` = offset
    ) |>
    req_retry(max_tries = 5) |>
    req_error(body = function(resp) resp_body_string(resp)) |>
    req_perform()

  rows <- resp_body_string(resp) |>
    jsonlite::fromJSON(simplifyVector = TRUE)
  if (length(rows) == 0) return(tibble())
  as_tibble(rows)
}

permit_pages <- list()
offset <- 0
repeat {
  page <- fetch_permits_page(offset)
  permit_pages[[length(permit_pages) + 1]] <- page
  message("offset ", offset, ": ", nrow(page), " rows")
  if (nrow(page) < permits_page_size) break
  offset <- offset + permits_page_size
}

    ISSUE_DATE = as.Date(substr(issue_date, 1, 10)),
    LATITUDE = as.numeric(latitude),

Build r5r street network
The street network comes from BBBike’s Chicago OSM extract (~100 MB, refreshed weekly), which covers lon −88.01 to −87.40 and lat 41.64 to 42.09. Every sale falls inside that box, so the statewide Illinois PBF (~350 MB) isn’t needed. The download is skipped if the file is already present, and r5r caches the built network next to it, so later runs only pay the build cost when the PBF changes.


Code
r5r_dir <- "data/r5r_chicago"
dir.create(r5r_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

pbf_url <- "https://download.bbbike.org/osm/bbbike/Chicago/Chicago.osm.pbf"
pbf <- file.path(r5r_dir, basename(pbf_url))
if (!file.exists(pbf)) {
  request(pbf_url) |>
    req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
    req_progress() |>
    req_perform(path = pbf)
}

Driving isochrones from the Loop
Driving-time isochrones from downtown Chicago (41.883249, -87.630944) at the cutoffs in isochrone_cutoffs. Note that r5r car routing uses free-flow speeds, so congestion isn’t modelled.


Downtown drive time for each sale
Car travel time from downtown to each sale’s own coordinates, routed with travel_time_matrix(). This replaces looking each sale up in the isochrones: the isochrones are drawn from a coarse grid and have holes wherever a grid point can’t be reached by car, which left 19 sales with NA. Routing each sale snaps it to the nearest drivable road instead.

downtown <- data.frame(id = "downtown", lat = 41.883249, lon = -87.630944)

# Many sales share coordinates, so route each unique location once.
# r5r needs an `id` column, which is renamed so it doesn't clash with all_sales$id
sale_pts <- all_sales |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  distinct(lon, lat) |>
  mutate(pt_id = as.character(row_number()))

downtown_tt <- travel_time_matrix(
  r5r_core,
  origins = downtown,
  destinations = rename(sale_pts, id = pt_id),
  mode = "CAR",
  departure_datetime = as.POSIXct("2023-10-04 08:00:00"),
  max_trip_duration = 90,
  progress = FALSE
)

all_sales <- all_sales |>
  select(-any_of("downtown_drive_time")) |>
  left_join(sale_pts, by = c("lon", "lat")) |>
  left_join(select(downtown_tt, pt_id = to_id, downtown_drive_time = travel_time_p50), by = "pt_id") |>
  select(-pt_id)

# LODES8 2023 Illinois OD, all jobs (JT00), all workers (S000). "main" keeps pairs where
# both home and work are in Illinois; lehdr caches the ~30 MB download.
lodes_args <- list(
  state = "il", year = 2023, version = "LODES8",
  lodes_type = "od", job_type = "JT00", segment = "S000",
  agg_geo = "block", state_part = "main", use_cache = TRUE
)

od_raw <- tryCatch(
  do.call(grab_lodes, lodes_args),
  error = function(e) {
    if (!grepl("outside the valid range", conditionMessage(e))) stop(e)
    # lehdr 1.2.0 hard-codes LODES8 years as 2002-2022 even though the 2023 release exists.
    # Reproduce what grab_lodes() does for that file: same URL, cache path and column types.
    message("lehdr rejected year 2023; downloading the LODES8 file directly instead")
    lodes_url <- "https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/lodes/LODES8/il/od/il_od_main_JT00_2023.csv.gz"
    lodes_cache <- tools::R_user_dir("lehdr", which = "cache")
    dir.create(lodes_cache, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
    lodes_file <- file.path(lodes_cache, paste0("lodes8_", basename(lodes_url)))
    if (!file.exists(lodes_file)) {
      request(lodes_url) |> req_retry(max_tries = 3) |> req_perform(path = lodes_file)
    }
    read_csv(lodes_file, col_types = cols(w_geocode = "c", h_geocode = "c", createdate = "c")) |>
      mutate(year = 2023L, state = "IL")
  }
)

First of all, we had to (pseudo) log-transform the scale because based on the summary of the residuals distribution, it is very skewed. To interpret the map:

Grey: model is accurate.
Red: model is underpredicting. At extreme values of red, model is severely underpredicting.

Our final model fails the worst at predicting house prices that are actually very high, especially those near the Loop. The model is guessing too low. We think this is because it is more difficult to predict for the range of a “very expensive” house, which is much larger than that of an average-priced house. Moreover, we assumed that a fixed effect spatial feature (e.g. distance to the Loop) would not need to be included in our model because it would be collinear with other similar “spatial” features like downtown drive time, which would have reflected similar patterns. In further iterations, we should include distance to the Loop.

Our model’s ratio, with a median of 0.998 differs by neighborhood income. The maximum ratio is 67 which is very high - this indicates predicted price was way overpredicted of the actual sale price.
However the highest ratio of 67 means that those houses are over-valued. This means that lower-income neighborhoods face disproportionate property tax-burden compared to higher-income neighborhoods. Conversely, luxury homes in higher-income areas often sell at premium prices that standard linear models under-predict (ratios below 1.0, like the 1st quartile of 0.743), leaving wealthier homeowners under-taxed.
This imbalance mirrors the core finding of The Tax Divide. Algorithmic and traditional assessment models routinely over-assess low-value properties while under-assessing high-value properties, creating a regressive tax structure.
In part 1, we cleaned out houses that cost over around $1800 per square foot, houses less than $20,000 and houses over $10 million. When we examined the standard deviation for price per square foot in the training dataset, three standard deviations away from the mean was 1800. We cleaned out 5 upper outliers this way that seemed way too far from the rest of our data set to accurately contribute to the model. Filtering out the low-end sales under $20k created an artificial price floor forcing the model to over-predict low-income home values that were outside of our model range. Simultaneously, removing luxury outliers (>$1800/sqft and >$10m) capped top-end predictions which led to under-assessment in these high-income neighborhoods. By trimming these extreme data anchors, the cleaning actually caused regressivity across both ends of the income spectrum.

(1) The model exhibits significant residual error and spatial bias. With an RMSE of $\$271,036$, individual property valuations can be off by hundreds of thousands of dollars. Furthermore, a Moran’s I of 0.270 indicates strong positive spatial autocorrelation, meaning the model’s errors are geographically clustered—it will systematically over-value or under-value entire neighborhoods rather than spreading errors randomly. Additionally, sparse extreme features create unrealistic coefficient swings (e.g., 12 bedrooms reducing predicted value by over $1.49M and 1 fireplace having a negative coefficient), making the model vulnerable to edge-case properties.
(2) There are many factors that influence a house’s sale price. We were able to explore many factors in this exercise through open-sources alone. However, there are a lot of proprietary datasets that are locked behind a paywall (i.e. GreatSchools for school ratings and performance). If the Assessor wants even further analysis done on predicting house sale prices, they may want to consider additional datasets.
(3) On the other hand, using too many factors could add unintended noise to the model. Given more time, we would test both more and fewer features to see their impact on our model.
